claim: The DNA Polymerase α (Pol α)/primase complex initiates DNA synthesis in eukaryotic replication.
source: The DNA Polymerase α (Pol α)/primase complex initiates DNA synthesis in eukaryotic replication.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a fundamental role of the complex.

claim: In the Pol α/primase complex, Pol α and primase cooperate in the production of RNA-DNA oligonucleotides that prime synthesis of new DNA.
source: In the complex, Pol α and primase cooperate in the production of RNA-DNA oligonucleotides that prime synthesis of new DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the functional cooperation between the two components.

claim: Crystal structures of the catalytic core of yeast Pol α were determined in unliganded form, bound to an RNA primer/DNA template, and extending an RNA primer with deoxynucleotides.
source: Here we report crystal structures of the catalytic core of yeast Pol α in unliganded form, bound to an RNA primer/DNA template and extending an RNA primer with deoxynucleotides.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the three structural forms that were crystallographically determined.

claim: Pol α specifically recognizes the A-form RNA/DNA helix.
source: We combine the structural analysis with biochemical and computational data to demonstrate that Pol α specifically recognizes the A-form RNA/DNA helix and that the ensuing synthesis of B-form DNA terminates primer synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding demonstrated through multiple approaches.

claim: The synthesis of B-form DNA by Pol α terminates primer synthesis.
source: We combine the structural analysis with biochemical and computational data to demonstrate that Pol α specifically recognizes the A-form RNA/DNA helix and that the ensuing synthesis of B-form DNA terminates primer synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a mechanism for primer termination.

claim: The Pol α/primase complex spontaneously releases the completed RNA-DNA primer.
source: The spontaneous release of the completed RNA-DNA primer by the Pol α/primase complex simplifies current models of primer transfer to leading- and lagging strand polymerases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding that impacts models of primer transfer.

claim: The mechanism of nucleotide polymerization by Pol α might contribute to genomic stability by limiting the amount of inaccurate DNA to be corrected at the start of each Okazaki fragment.
source: The proposed mechanism of nucleotide polymerization by Pol α might contribute to genomic stability by limiting the amount of inaccurate DNA to be corrected at the start of each Okazaki fragment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a proposed functional consequence of the mechanism.

claim: Cellular organisms initiate DNA synthesis during genome duplication by the universal mechanism of RNA priming.
source: Cellular organisms initiate DNA synthesis during genome duplication by the universal mechanism of RNA priming, the assembly of short RNA molecules on the unwound strands of the DNA helix by a specialized DNA-dependent RNA polymerase known as primase (Frick and Richardson, 2001; Kuchta and Stengel, 2010; DePamphilis and Bell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RNA primers are extended in an obligate 5′ to 3′ direction by replicative DNA polymerases.
source: The RNA primers are extended in an obligate 5′ to 3′ direction by the replicative DNA polymerases that synthesize the bulk of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a fundamental property of DNA synthesis.

claim: The repeated priming events necessary for discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand require constant activity of primase at the replication fork.
source: The repeated priming events necessary for the discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand require the constant activity of primase at the replication fork.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the requirements for lagging strand synthesis.

claim: In bacteria and bacteriophages, RNA priming is performed by a single-chain primase acting in combination with the replicative helicase.
source: In bacteria and bacteriophages, RNA priming is performed by a single-chain primase, acting in combination with the replicative helicase, to which it is bound by a dynamic interaction or is fused together in the same polypeptide (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The eukaryotic primase is a heterodimer of catalytic and regulatory subunits.
source: The eukaryotic primase is a heterodimer of catalytic and regulatory subunits that is associated with the catalytic subunit of Pol α and its accessory B subunit in a constitutive heterotetrameric assembly, the Pol α/primase complex (Loeb et al., 1986; Kaguni and Lehman, 1988; Foiani et al., 1997; Lao-Sirieix et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The Pol α/primase complex is a constitutive heterotetrameric assembly.
source: The eukaryotic primase is a heterodimer of catalytic and regulatory subunits that is associated with the catalytic subunit of Pol α and its accessory B subunit in a constitutive heterotetrameric assembly, the Pol α/primase complex (Loeb et al., 1986; Kaguni and Lehman, 1988; Foiani et al., 1997; Lao-Sirieix et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The Pol α/primase complex is an integral component of the eukaryotic replisome.
source: Reflecting its critical importance to DNA replication, the Pol α/primase complex is an integral component of the eukaryotic replisome (Calzada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Oligonucleotides synthesized by bacterial and bacteriophage primases are between 4 and 12 nucleotides long and made exclusively of RNA.
source: The oligonucleotides synthesized by bacterial and bacteriophage primases are between 4 and 12 nucleotides long and made exclusively of RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of bacterial/bacteriophage primers.

claim: The Pol α/primase complex produces composite RNA-DNA primers that result from the concerted enzymatic activities of primase and Pol α.
source: In contrast, the Pol α/primase complex produces longer, composite RNA-DNA primers that result from the concerted enzymatic activities of primase and Pol α (Chang et al., 1984; Hu et al., 1984; Singh, et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Primer synthesis by the Pol α/primase complex involves initiation, extension and completion of RNA synthesis by primase, intramolecular hand-off of the RNA oligonucleotide to Pol α, and limited RNA extension with deoxynucleotides.
source: Detailed knowledge of the mechanism of primer synthesis is lacking, but it must involves initiation, extension and completion of RNA synthesis by primase, intramolecular hand-off of the RNA oligonucleotide to Pol α and limited RNA extension with deoxynucleotides (dNTPs) (Brooks and Dumas, 1989; Kuchta et al., 1990; Copeland and Wang, 1993; Sheaff and Kuchta, 1993; Sheaff et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The large subunit of primase performs a critical function in the primer initiation step via its Fe-S domain.
source: The large subunit of primase performs a critical function in the primer initiation step via its Fe-S domain (Klinge et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2007), whereas the B subunit of Pol α lacks enzymatic activity and likely acts as a scaffold to mediate interactions with other components of the replicative apparatus (Uchiyama and Wang, 2004; Klinge et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The B subunit of Pol α lacks enzymatic activity and likely acts as a scaffold to mediate interactions with other components of the replicative apparatus.
source: The large subunit of primase performs a critical function in the primer initiation step via its Fe-S domain (Klinge et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2007), whereas the B subunit of Pol α lacks enzymatic activity and likely acts as a scaffold to mediate interactions with other components of the replicative apparatus (Uchiyama and Wang, 2004; Klinge et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: After completion of primer synthesis by Pol α/primase, the primer is elongated by the processive Pols δ and ε that synthesize the majority of chromosomal DNA on the lagging and leading strand templates, respectively.
source: After completion of primer synthesis by Pol α/primase, the primer is elongated by the processive Pols δ and ε that synthesize the majority of chromosomal DNA on the lagging and leading strand templates, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the subsequent steps after priming.

claim: Before ligation of completed Okazaki fragments, the RNA portion of the primer is excised by specific nucleases such as Fen1 and Dna2.
source: Before ligation of the completed Okazaki fragments, the RNA portion of the primer is excised by specific nucleases such as Fen1 and Dna2 (Burgers, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Pol α lacks proofreading activity.
source: The composite nature of the RNA-DNA primers poses a special challenge to the eukaryotic replication apparatus, that must further correct the DNA segment synthesized by Pol α, which lacks proofreading activity; current evidence indicates that the DNA portion of the primer might be corrected by Pol δ (Pavlov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of Pol α.

claim: Current evidence indicates that the DNA portion of the primer might be corrected by Pol δ.
source: The composite nature of the RNA-DNA primers poses a special challenge to the eukaryotic replication apparatus, that must further correct the DNA segment synthesized by Pol α, which lacks proofreading activity; current evidence indicates that the DNA portion of the primer might be corrected by Pol δ (Pavlov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The catalytic core of yeast Pol α comprises amino acids 349–1258 (910 amino acids).
source: We have determined crystal structures of the catalytic core (349–1258; 910 amino acids) of yeast Pol α in unliganded form (apo), bound to an RNA primer/DNA template duplex (binary complex) and in a productive complex with RNA primer/DNA template and incoming dGTP (ternary complex).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structural studies.

claim: A polymerase mutant (D998N) with attenuated catalytic activity was used for structural studies of the ternary complex.
source: For structural studies of the ternary complex, we used a polymerase mutant (D998N) with attenuated catalytic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: During crystallization of the ternary complex, the polymerase extended the 3′-end of the RNA primer by addition of two deoxyguanosine nucleotides.
source: During crystallization of the ternary complex, the polymerase extended the 3′-end of the RNA primer by addition of two deoxyguanosine nucleotides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The crystal structure captures the actively copying Pol α in the act of extending the RNA primer with deoxynucleotides.
source: Thus, our crystal structure captures the actively copying Pol α in the act of extending the RNA primer with deoxynucleotides (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–4, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The catalytic region of Pol α adopts the universal 'right-hand' DNA polymerase fold consisting of a palm domain, a fingers domain, and a thumb domain.
source: The catalytic region of Pol α adopts the universal 'right-hand' DNA polymerase fold consisting of a palm domain harboring the active site, a fingers domain that interacts with the incoming nucleotide and a thumb domain that grips the primer-template duplex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the overall structure.

claim: Pol α is the prototypical member of the B-family of DNA polymerases.
source: As the prototypical member of the B-family of DNA polymerases, distinctive structural features that had been identified previously in bacteriophage RB69 Pol (Wang et al., 1997), bacterial DNA Pol II (Wang and Yang, 2009) and yeast Pol δ (Swan et al., 2009), such as the extended N-terminal region or the antiparallel hairpin fold of the helical fingers domain, are also present in Pol α.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The majority of the contacts of the polymerase with the primer/template duplex takes place within a region of 7 bp from the 3′-terminus of the templated primer.
source: The majority of the contacts of the polymerase with the primer/template duplex takes place within a region of 7 bp from the 3′-terminus of the templated primer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pol α's footprint on the primer-template duplex is smaller than normally observed in B-family DNA polymerases.
source: Pol α's footprint on the primer-template duplex is smaller than normally observed in B-family DNA polymerases and matches the minimal primer size that is efficiently utilized by the polymerase (Kuchta et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Pol α's footprint on the primer-template duplex matches the minimal primer size that is efficiently utilized by the polymerase.
source: Pol α's footprint on the primer-template duplex is smaller than normally observed in B-family DNA polymerases and matches the minimal primer size that is efficiently utilized by the polymerase (Kuchta et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Four deoxynucleotides of single-stranded DNA template fit in extended conformation within the groove formed by the exonuclease domain and N-terminal region of Pol α.
source: Four deoxynucleotides of single-stranded DNA template fit in extended conformation within the groove formed by the exonuclease domain and N-terminal region of Pol α, in agreement with the position of template DNA upstream of the active site previously observed in other B-family DNA polymerases (Hogg et al., 2007; Swan, et al., 2009; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and shown in a figure.

claim: The RNA primer–DNA template helix bound to Pol α adopts overall an A-DNA conformation.
source: The RNA primer–DNA template helix bound to Pol α adopts overall an A-DNA conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Clustering analysis identifies a continuous stretch of six dinucleotide steps as A-DNA and one step as B-DNA flanked by dinucleotides in A-like conformation in the RNA/DNA helix bound to Pol α.
source: Clustering analysis for each dinucleotide step of the mean z-coordinates of the phosphorus atoms with the glycosyl torsion angle χ (Lu et al., 2000) identifies a continuous stretch of six dinucleotide steps as A-DNA and one step as B-DNA flanked by dinucleotides in A-like conformation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a citation and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The palm and thumb domains of actively copying DNA polymerases make continuous contact with the minor groove of the primer-template DNA over a full turn of the DNA double helix.
source: Extensive structural analysis has demonstrated that the palm and thumb domains of actively copying DNA polymerases make continuous contact with the minor groove of the primer-template DNA over a full turn of the DNA double helix.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge from structural studies.

claim: The palm domain of Pol α makes a canonical set of interactions with the first 3 bp of the primer-template helix.
source: Strikingly, the structure of Pol α bound productively to RNA primer/DNA template shows that, although the palm domain makes a canonical set of interactions with the first 3 bp of the primer-template helix, the thumb domain engages almost exclusively with the RNA primer strand (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The thumb domain of Pol α engages almost exclusively with the RNA primer strand.
source: Strikingly, the structure of Pol α bound productively to RNA primer/DNA template shows that, although the palm domain makes a canonical set of interactions with the first 3 bp of the primer-template helix, the thumb domain engages almost exclusively with the RNA primer strand (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The interactions between the thumb domain and the RNA primer are concentrated in a contiguous region of five nucleotides, from position two to six of the RNA primer.
source: The interactions between the thumb domain and the RNA primer are concentrated in a contiguous region of five nucleotides, from position two to six of the RNA primer and involve solely the ribose and phosphate moieties of the RNA backbone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The interactions between the thumb domain and the RNA primer involve solely the ribose and phosphate moieties of the RNA backbone.
source: The interactions between the thumb domain and the RNA primer are concentrated in a contiguous region of five nucleotides, from position two to six of the RNA primer and involve solely the ribose and phosphate moieties of the RNA backbone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pol α exploits the wide, shallow nature of the minor groove of the RNA/DNA helix with a series of hydrophobic contacts involving the side chains of Met1131, Leu1133, Tyr1140, Pro1141, Met1146.
source: Pol α exploits the wide, shallow nature of the minor groove of the RNA/DNA helix with a series of hydrophobic contacts involving the side chains of Met1131, Leu1133, Tyr1140, Pro1141, Met1146, which recognize the C3′-endo conformation of the ribose moieties of RNA nucleotides in position four to six (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The hydrophobic contacts of the thumb domain recognize the C3′-endo conformation of the ribose moieties of RNA nucleotides in position four to six.
source: Pol α exploits the wide, shallow nature of the minor groove of the RNA/DNA helix with a series of hydrophobic contacts involving the side chains of Met1131, Leu1133, Tyr1140, Pro1141, Met1146, which recognize the C3′-endo conformation of the ribose moieties of RNA nucleotides in position four to six (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The side chain of Arg1075 extends into the minor groove and packs its guanidinium moiety against the ribose sugar of Ade4.
source: The side chain of Arg1075 extends into the minor groove and packs its guanidinium moiety against the ribose sugar of Ade4 (Figures 2C and 3A), thus engaging in an interaction that matches closely the contact made by the equivalent Arg839 of yeast Pol δ with the DNA primer (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: The close contact with Arg1075 induces a local rearrangement of the RNA conformation, which includes a B-DNA C2′-endo ribose pucker for Ade4 and unstacking between the aromatic bases of nucleotides four and five.
source: However, in the case of Pol α the close contact with Arg1075 induces a local rearrangement of the RNA conformation, which includes a B-DNA C2′-endo ribose pucker for Ade4 and unstacking between the aromatic bases of nucleotides four and five (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The local conformation of the RNA primer is stabilized by insertion of the Arg1076 side chain between the phosphate groups of nucleotides three and four.
source: The local conformation of the RNA primer is stabilized by insertion of the Arg1076 side chain between the phosphate groups of nucleotides three and four (Figures 2C and 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2C and 3C,D.

claim: The 'snap-clip' interaction of arginines 1075 and 1076 with the RNA backbone anchors the RNA primer to the thumb domain of Pol α.
source: The 'snap-clip' interaction of arginines 1075 and 1076 with the RNA backbone anchors the RNA primer to the thumb domain of Pol α, by facilitating the formation of three hydrogen bonds between the phosphate groups of nucleotides four, five and six and the mainchain nitrogens of residues Arg1076, Lys1132 and Ser1134, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The G1116E mutation in fission yeast Pol α at the equivalent position to Ser1134 causes a defect in mating-type switching.
source: The G1116E mutation in fission yeast Pol α at the equivalent position to Ser1134 causes a defect in mating-type switching (Singh and Klar, 1993): the close interaction of Ser1134 with the RNA primer suggests that the defect might be caused by weakened affinity of Pol α for its primer-template substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The defect caused by the G1116E mutation might be caused by weakened affinity of Pol α for its primer-template substrate.
source: The G1116E mutation in fission yeast Pol α at the equivalent position to Ser1134 causes a defect in mating-type switching (Singh and Klar, 1993): the close interaction of Ser1134 with the RNA primer suggests that the defect might be caused by weakened affinity of Pol α for its primer-template substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural data.

claim: Pol α displayed only weak activity and limited processivity when extending a DNA primer.
source: Whereas Pol α displayed only weak activity and limited processivity when extending a DNA primer, extension of an RNA primer resulted in much higher levels of polymerization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Extension of an RNA primer by Pol α resulted in much higher levels of polymerization compared to DNA primer extension.
source: Whereas Pol α displayed only weak activity and limited processivity when extending a DNA primer, extension of an RNA primer resulted in much higher levels of polymerization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The profile of RNA-dependent extension products showed a pronounced peak at between 10 to 12 nucleotides, indicating strong processivity limited to a full-turn of double helix.
source: Strikingly, the profile of RNA-dependent extension products showed a pronounced peak at between 10 to 12 nucleotides, indicating strong processivity limited to a full-turn of double helix (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The characteristics of the catalytic activity of Pol α were observed for the isolated polymerase core as well as the Pol α/primase complex and are independent of primer size.
source: Such characteristics of the catalytic activity of Pol α were observed for the isolated polymerase core as well as the Pol α /primase complex and are independent of primer size (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Short runs of consecutive deoxyguanosine nucleotides can induce A-like DNA conformation in double-stranded DNA.
source: It is known that, although double-stranded DNA normally adopts a B-DNA conformation, its structure can display pronounced conformational variation depending on the local sequence of bases. Short runs of consecutive deoxyguanosine nucleotides can induce A-like DNA conformation in double-stranded DNA (Svozil et al., 2008; Marathe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: As the deoxyguanosine content of the DNA primer increased, the size profile of the extension products synthesized by Pol α changed from that expected of a DNA primer to that of an RNA primer.
source: Indeed, as the deoxyguanosine content of the DNA primer increased, the size profile of the extension products synthesized by Pol α changed from that expected of a DNA primer to that of an RNA primer (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Extension of the RNA primer is limited to a single turn of double helix.
source: The observation that extension of the RNA primer is limited to a single turn of double helix indicates that termination of primer synthesis might be triggered by the loss of specific interactions of Pol α with the RNA/DNA duplex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental observations.

claim: Termination of primer synthesis might be triggered by the loss of specific interactions of Pol α with the RNA/DNA duplex.
source: The observation that extension of the RNA primer is limited to a single turn of double helix indicates that termination of primer synthesis might be triggered by the loss of specific interactions of Pol α with the RNA/DNA duplex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: In order to adopt the conformation observed in ternary complex, the thumb domain of Pol α must rotate inwards by about 20°.
source: In order to adopt the conformation observed in ternary complex, the thumb domain of Pol α must rotate inwards by about 20°, a large conformational rearrangement compared for instance with the limited movement of the thumb domain observed in structures of isolated and copying RB69 Pol (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The thumb domain rotation in Pol α is a large conformational rearrangement compared with the limited movement observed in structures of isolated and copying RB69 Pol.
source: In order to adopt the conformation observed in ternary complex, the thumb domain of Pol α must rotate inwards by about 20°, a large conformational rearrangement compared for instance with the limited movement of the thumb domain observed in structures of isolated and copying RB69 Pol (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of the interactions with the primer-template duplex would allow the thumb domain to rotate away from the DNA, terminating the productive engagement of the polymerase with its substrate.
source: The large difference in the position of the thumb domain in the ternary complex and in the isolated polymerase suggests a molecular basis for the release of the completed primer-template by Pol α: loss of the interactions with the primer-template duplex would allow the thumb domain to rotate away from the DNA, terminating the productive engagement of the polymerase with its substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from structural comparisons.

claim: The actively copying polymerase maintains a stable conformation over the 100 ns duration of the simulation.
source: Principal component analysis of the trajectories shows that the actively copying polymerase maintains a stable conformation over the 100 ns duration of the simulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The structure of the isolated polymerase displays considerable conformational fluctuations, indicative of large-scale conformational changes and local loss of secondary structure that affect in particular the N-amino terminal region and the thumb domain.
source: In comparison, the structure of the isolated polymerase displays considerable conformational fluctuations, indicative of large-scale conformational changes and local loss of secondary structure that affect in particular the N-amino terminal region and the thumb domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The conformational flexibility of the isolated polymerase does not seem to be sufficient to sample conformations adopted by the polymerase in the ternary complex.
source: Importantly, the conformational flexibility of the isolated polymerase does not seem to be sufficient to sample conformations adopted by the polymerase in the ternary complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The trajectory of the polymerase starting from the ternary complex conformation but without RNA/DNA and dGTP showed an increased conformational instability, accompanied by a tendency to relax towards the apo conformation.
source: The trajectory showed an increased conformational instability, accompanied by a tendency to relax towards the apo conformation of the polymerase (Figure 5C and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulations and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pol α reaches the active conformation observed in the ternary complex via an 'induced fit' mechanism that is dependent on its interactions with the RNA/DNA duplex and deoxynucleotide.
source: Taken together, the results of the molecular dynamics simulations indicate that Pol α reaches the active conformation observed in the ternary complex via an 'induced fit' mechanism that is dependent on its interactions with the RNA/DNA duplex and deoxynucleotide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Loss of the optimal set of protein-RNA contacts would weaken the grip of the polymerase on its primer/template substrate and promote primer release.
source: Loss of the optimal set of protein-RNA contacts would weaken the grip of the polymerase on its primer/template substrate and promote primer release.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Adoption of a conformation competent for catalysis by DNA polymerases requires the concerted movements of the fingers domain and the thumb domain.
source: It is well established that adoption of a conformation competent for catalysis by DNA polymerases requires the concerted movements of the fingers domain, that rotates upwards to form the nucleotide binding site, and of the thumb domain, that embraces the primer-template duplex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: As the polymerase morphs from the apo to the active conformation, the palm domain tilts away from the rising fingers, by rotating on the short helix containing the highly conserved 864-DFNSLYPS-871 motif.
source: Comparison of Pol α structures in the apo, binary and ternary complex reveals a further and unexpected rearrangement: as the polymerase morphs from the apo to the active conformation, the palm domain tilts away from the rising fingers, by rotating on the short helix containing the highly conserved 864-DFNSLYPS-871 motif, known as region II of B-family DNA polymerases (Wang et al., 1989; Delarue et al., 1990; Hubscher et al., 2002; Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and shown in figures.

claim: Rotation of the palm domain is accompanied by a conformational rearrangement of region II that is necessary in order to accommodate the phosphoribose moiety of the incoming nucleotide.
source: Rotation of the palm domain is accompanied by a conformational rearrangement of region II that is necessary in order to accommodate the phosphoribose moiety of the incoming nucleotide (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two copies of binary complex present in the asymmetric unit of the crystals capture intermediate states of the transition.
source: The two copies of binary complex present in the asymmetric unit of the crystals capture intermediate states of the transition, as in one binary complex the conformation of region II is apo-like, whereas in the second copy region II adopts a conformation akin to that observed in the ternary complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on crystallographic observations.

claim: The observed movement of the palm domain could participate in a 'ratchet' mechanism for unidirectional translocation of Pol α.
source: The observed movement of the palm domain could participate in a 'ratchet' mechanism for unidirectional translocation of Pol α, as return of the palm domain to the apo conformation after catalysis would propel the polymerase forward onto the next templating base.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Site-specific mutations of Ser863 in region II of human Pol α cause a drastic reduction in the specific activity of the polymerase without changing its kinetic parameters.
source: Interestingly, site-specific mutations of Ser863 in region II of human Pol α (Ser867 of yeast Pol α), which acts as the pivot during rotation of the palm domain, cause a drastic reduction in the specific activity of the polymerase without changing its kinetic parameters, in agreement with a potential structural role of this serine residue in DNA polymerisation (Dong et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Recognition of the intrinsic and induced geometry of the RNA/DNA helix by Pol α would prompt rapid dNTP polymerization, until a full turn of DNA double helix has been synthesized.
source: Recognition of the intrinsic and induced geometry of the RNA/DNA helix by Pol α would prompt rapid dNTP polymerization, until a full turn of DNA double helix has been synthesized.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Translocation away from the RNA/DNA helix and synthesis of B-form DNA would cause Pol α to stall.
source: Translocation away from the RNA/DNA helix and synthesis of B-form DNA would cause Pol α to stall, akin to a locomotive running into railtrack of different gauge.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Loss of the optimal interface contacts between Pol α and the primer-template helix would favor a conformational change towards the apo conformation of the polymerase, with consequent disengagement of Pol α from the completed RNA-DNA primer.
source: Loss of the optimal interface contacts between Pol α and the primer-template helix would favor a conformational change towards the apo conformation of the polymerase, with consequent disengagement of Pol α from the completed RNA-DNA primer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Spontaneous primer release once a helical equivalent of deoxynucleotides has been added to the RNA primer would make the 3′-terminus of the RNA-DNA primer directly available for extension by Pol δ and Pol ε.
source: Spontaneous primer release once a helical equivalent of deoxynucleotides has been added to the RNA primer would make the 3′-terminus of the RNA-DNA primer directly available for extension by Pol δ and Pol ε, the DNA polymerases that synthesize the bulk of genomic DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: The mechanism of primer release by Pol α removes the need for molecular transactions between primer-bound Pol α and the replicative apparatus deputed to leading and lagging strand synthesis.
source: Such a mechanism provides a straightforward model of primer hand-off in eukaryotic replication, by removing the need for molecular transactions between primer-bound Pol α and the replicative apparatus deputed to leading and lagging strand synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an implication of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The mechanism of primer release by Pol α is conceptually similar to the mechanism of polymerase switching proposed for Pol η after lesion by-pass.
source: We note that, although the molecular details differ, the mechanism of primer release by Pol α described here is conceptually similar to the mechanism of polymerase switching proposed for Pol η after lesion by-pass (Biertumpfel et al., 2010; Silverstein et al., 2010): for both polymerases, termination of DNA synthesis appears to be a direct consequence of the specific way in which they interact with their nucleic acid substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The ability of primases to synthesise RNA primers of discrete size has been well characterized.
source: The ability of primases to synthesise RNA primers of discrete size has been well characterized (Kuchta and Stengel, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Extension of an RNA primer by Pol α leads to controlled termination of synthesis, in a functionally analogous manner to the known counting ability of primase.
